strengths: Significance: Learning flexible encoders for arbitrary modality subsets addresses a useful problem. The combination of masked objectives, permutation-invariant aggregation, mixture distributions, and private latent variables offers a coherent framework for multimodal VAEs.

Originality: The strongest contribution is the synthesis and analysis of existing ideas, especially the conditional aggregated-posterior interpretation and the comparison of likelihood, reconstruction, and representation-learning trade-offs.

Empirical evidence: The experiments vary objectives and aggregation schemes separately, include analytically evaluable linear models, and examine missing modalities and latent recovery. The parameter-expanded PoE+/MoE+ controls on MNIST-SVHN-Text help assess whether improvements merely reflect additional capacity.

Presentation and limitations: The paper explicitly acknowledges that its objective is only an approximate likelihood bound, discusses additional computational cost, and reports settings where mixture-based objectives perform better. Architecture tables, pseudocode, and benchmark training settings provide useful implementation detail. No material research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness: Remark 5 states an unconditional entropy lower bound on the mixture objective's likelihood gap that is false under the stated model class. For independent standard-Gaussian modalities with decoders that ignore z and q(z|x_S)=p(z), the mixture ELBO equals log p(x), while H(X_complement|X_S)>0. The displayed inequality is therefore violated. Additional assumptions or a corrected result are needed because this claim directly motivates the proposed objective.

Soundness: Corollary 2 contains a residual expectation with unrestricted sign. Exact posterior encoders make the objective tight, but encoder capacity alone does not establish that joint optimization will reach this condition, nor that the objective is tighter than the baseline at learned parameters. The manuscript acknowledges the approximation but supplies neither a finite-error guarantee nor measurements of this residual in its analytically tractable experiments.

Technical correctness and reproducibility: Several equations and algorithms are inconsistent. Proposition 1's Xconditional identity has the opposite sign for the log(q(z|x_S)/p(z|x_S)) correction from Corollary 2 and the Appendix A derivation. Algorithm 2 subtracts the private-posterior log density twice, omits the corresponding shared-posterior denominator, and writes the conditional reconstruction without the required private latents. These affect implementation, rather than merely typography, and undermine confidence in the private-latent results.

Evaluation: Nonlinear likelihood comparisons use each model's own learned encoder as an importance proposal, with 64 particles in Table 3 and 512 in Table 5. Finite-sample log-importance estimates have proposal-dependent downward bias, so better inference can improve the reported estimate without improving the generative likelihood. Particle-count convergence, effective-sample-size diagnostics, or an independent evaluation proposal are needed to substantiate the central likelihood claim beyond the linear experiments.

Evaluation and significance: Table 1 retains a numerically failed PoE baseline with reconstruction and rate magnitudes around 10^35. This cannot support a meaningful architectural comparison without diagnosing and stabilizing the baseline. Benefits are also qualified elsewhere: equivariant PoE has higher MCC than the learned aggregators in Table 2, and the proposed objective reduces several cross-modal coherence scores in Table 6. The useful contribution is narrower than a general improvement in latent recovery or multimodal generation.

Originality and theoretical scope: The objective explicitly generalizes Wu and Goodman (2019), the aggregation networks instantiate DeepSets and Set Transformers, and Proposition 15 follows an existing identifiability theorem. That proposition assumes exact exponential-family posteriors and injective complementary decoders; it does not establish that the proposed training procedure satisfies these conditions. The methodological and identifiability advances should be distinguished more precisely from these inherited results.

Presentation and reproducibility: Despite extensive appendices, implementation details remain inconsistent: Section 5.2 specifies latent dimension 10 for the five-modality nonlinear experiment, whereas Table 18 specifies 25; Table 15's modality encoder outputs 60 features while its aggregation network expects 256. Synthetic optimization settings and several repetition counts are unclear. Correcting these discrepancies and providing a runnable implementation are necessary before others can reliably reproduce the findings.

strengths: Significance: Learning encoders for arbitrary modality subsets is a useful problem. Combining modality-specific features with DeepSets or Set Transformers provides a practical alternative to fixed PoE/MoE aggregation, including extensions for private latent variables and mixture distributions.

Empirical evidence: The experiments separate the training objective from the aggregation architecture, include analytical likelihood evaluation for linear models, and introduce larger PoE+/MoE+ baselines to address parameter-count confounding. Tables 3–5 show promising likelihood improvements in several settings.

Originality: The connection between subset-conditioned inference, conditional consistency, and marginal/conditional rate–distortion quantities offers a potentially useful synthesis, even though its architectural and variational ingredients largely come from existing work.

Presentation, reproducibility, and limitations: The manuscript supplies extensive architecture descriptions, pseudocode, and benchmark training settings. It explicitly acknowledges that the objective is not always a lower bound, increased computational cost, and weaker cross-reconstruction performance. These candid limitations are appropriate; no material research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness—an important comparison theorem is false as stated. Remark 5 claims that the mixture objective necessarily has a likelihood gap at least H(X_complement | X_S). Consider independent standard-Gaussian modalities with decoders that ignore z and encoders equal to the prior. Then the mixture ELBO equals the exact log-likelihood for every subset, while the stated conditional entropy is strictly positive. Additional assumptions or a corrected result are necessary. This directly affects the theoretical motivation for superiority over mixture-based bounds.

Soundness—the central derivations contain substantive inconsistencies. In Proposition 1, the expected log(q(z|x_S)/p(z|x_S)) correction in Xconditional has the opposite sign from the correct expansion and Corollary 2. Appendix A also gives a difference of KL terms where the chain rule requires their sum. These may be repairable errors, but they occur in the main distribution-matching argument and prevent accepting the analysis as verified.

Soundness—the title's tighter-bound interpretation is insufficiently established. Corollary 2 correctly exposes an unsigned correction, and Remark 3 acknowledges that the objective can exceed the log-likelihood. However, encoder capacity alone does not establish that joint optimization attains the required posterior or conditional-consistency conditions. The paper provides neither a general ordering against the mixture objective nor measurements showing that this correction is controlled in the reported experiments. Attainable tightness under ideal conditions should be distinguished from a demonstrated tighter training bound.

Reproducibility—the private-latent algorithm is incorrect as written. Algorithm 2 subtracts the full private-encoder log density twice, omits the corresponding full shared-encoder log-density term, and writes the reconstruction without the private latents needed by the stated decoder. This does not implement the advertised conditional KL. The manuscript does not provide an identifiable release of its implementation that would resolve whether these are transcription errors or affect the experiments.

Evaluation—the nonlinear likelihood comparisons conflate generative-model quality with inference quality. Appendix I uses each model's own encoder as its importance proposal, with 64 particles in Table 3 and 512 in Table 5. Finite-sample log estimates have proposal-dependent downward bias, so better encoders can improve reported likelihood without an equivalent improvement in the underlying model likelihood. Particle-count convergence, effective-sample-size diagnostics, or an independent evaluation proposal are needed. The exact linear-model evaluation is valuable but does not settle this concern for the nonlinear results.

Evaluation—baseline reliability needs further investigation. Table 1 reports PoE reconstruction and rate magnitudes around 10^35, making that comparison primarily evidence of numerical failure. Moreover, Section 3 prints an incorrect Gaussian PoE mean using covariance-weighted rather than precision-weighted expert means. These issues do not prove the implementation is wrong, but they warrant an implementation check and stable reruns before drawing conclusions about PoE's limitations.

Significance and originality—the demonstrated advance remains narrower than the manuscript's breadth suggests. The objective explicitly generalizes Wu and Goodman (2019), the aggregation networks are established set architectures, and Proposition 15 transfers an existing conditional-identifiability result while assuming exact posterior representation. Its assumptions are not established for the general mixture-prior experiments. Beyond simulations, evaluation is limited to MNIST–SVHN–Text, where coherence and representation quality show substantial trade-offs rather than consistent gains. The synthesis has merit, but the unresolved theoretical and evaluation issues outweigh that contribution.

strengths: Significance: Flexible inference from arbitrary modality subsets is a useful problem. Combining modality-specific feature extractors with permutation-invariant aggregation provides a practical alternative to fixed PoE/MoE schemes, including extensions to mixture distributions and private latent variables.

Originality: The strongest contribution is the unified understanding of marginal fitting, conditional consistency, and rate–distortion trade-offs. The connection between the masked objective and flexible aggregation is useful, although its ingredients build on established methods.

Empirical merits: The experiments separately vary objectives and aggregation schemes, include analytical likelihood evaluation in linear models, and introduce parameter-matched PoE+/MoE+ controls on MNIST-SVHN-Text. These controls provide meaningful evidence beyond comparisons against published baseline numbers.

Presentation and limitations: The manuscript explicitly acknowledges that the objective is only an approximate lower bound, discusses computational costs, and reports cases where mixture objectives improve cross-reconstruction or classification. These qualifications are valuable. The described synthetic and standard benchmark experiments raise no apparent material ethical concerns.
weaknesses: Soundness: Important mathematical statements are inconsistent. In Proposition 1, the Xconditional identity places the expectation of log(q(z|xS)/p(z|xS)) under a minus sign; it should contribute positively, as it does in Corollary 2. Appendix A also incorrectly subtracts the reconstruction KL in its final conditional decomposition. These errors affect the central distribution-matching analysis and require a systematic correction.

Soundness and reproducibility: Algorithm 2 does not implement the stated private-latent objective as written. Its conditional term subtracts the private-posterior log density twice, omits the corresponding shared-posterior subtraction, and evaluates reconstruction without the private latent inputs required by the generative model. Without an inspectable implementation, it is unclear whether the experiments used the intended objective.

Evidence for likelihood improvements is incomplete. Tables 3–5 estimate log likelihood using each model's own encoder with only 64 or 512 importance samples. These estimates have proposal-dependent finite-sample bias, so improved encoders can improve the reported estimate without a corresponding improvement in the generative distribution. Particle-count convergence, effective sample sizes, or independently strengthened evaluation proposals are needed. The analytical linear experiments help, but do not resolve this issue for the nonlinear results.

Theoretical scope: Corollary 2 establishes equality when inference is exact, but supplies no quantitative control of the potentially positive correction under approximate inference. Infinite encoder capacity alone does not establish that joint optimization reaches this condition. Proposition 15 transfers an existing conditional identifiability result under exact-posterior, exponential-family, injectivity, and variability assumptions; the experiments do not establish that these assumptions hold for the learned models.

Reproducibility and presentation remain below acceptance quality despite extensive appendices. Table 15 makes modality encoders output 60 dimensions while aggregation expects 256; Section 5.2 specifies latent dimension 10 while Table 18 specifies 25. Training details for synthetic experiments are incomplete, and no implementation release is identified. These inconsistencies prevent unambiguous reconstruction of the experiments.

The practical evidence has limited reach: evaluation centers on synthetic data and one constructed digit benchmark, with no runtime measurements supporting scalability. Table 1's PoE baseline exhibits quantities around 10^35, indicating numerical failure rather than a reliable comparison. The useful conceptual contribution does not outweigh the unresolved mathematical, implementation, and evaluation concerns.
